name: Nora Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run filler line three at Brookfield Drinks, a soft-drinks bottling plant on the edge of town. Line three does 30,000 bottles an hour, so my day is changeovers, clearing jams at the capper, checking fill heights and keeping the labeller happy. I'm on earlies this month, six till two.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love a clean changeover, going from lemon to cola in under forty minutes when everyone's in sync. What wears me out is the labeller, which jams if the glue is a degree too cold, and the ringing in my ears at night. And standing on concrete for eight hours, my feet feel thirty years older than me.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My fiancé Tom is a joiner, he fits kitchens and staircases. We rent a terrace on Station Street, and the wedding's next August at my church, where I sing in the choir. We've got about four months of bills saved, but the wedding is eating into it. I'm also doing an online course at night on PLCs, the little computers that run the line, with an AI tutor on my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first of five pictures of the future. This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. That would be a bit of a letdown, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably post something jokey, like all that hype and my labeller still jams. At work I'd remind the operators on line two that I told them not to worry. Mostly I'd shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it'd be fine. I'd keep using the AI tools for what they're good at, which is explaining fault codes and helping me study, and I'd keep moving toward a technician job. Brookfield is busy, summer orders keep going up, and the plant isn't going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the PLC course by March and apply for the line technician post when Sandra Mensah, my shift manager, opens it in spring. Tom and I would pay for the wedding as we go, so we don't touch the four months saved. I'd keep using my phone AI every day, it's like having a patient teacher in my pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit cheated, maybe, because I've bet on this stuff and I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the wedding is eating into your savings. How tight is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight but planned. The church hall is booked, my aunt is doing the cake, and Tom is building our wedding arch himself from oak offcuts. My dad always said debt for a day is debt for years, so my fiancé Tom and I will never borrow for the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI stays a handy tool, what does it actually do for you on the line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week the labeller threw an error code nobody on shift knew. The chatbot told me the labeller fault was glue temperature, and we were running again in ten minutes instead of waiting an hour for the engineer. That's the whole value, and it's plenty for me.

say: I'd post a **jokey line** that the hype ended and my labeller still jams.
I'd remind the operators on **line two** that I told them not to worry.
think: Brookfield is **busy**, with summer orders rising, so the plant feels safe.
AI stays useful for **fault codes** and study, which suits me fine.
do: Finish the **PLC course** by March and apply for line technician in spring.
Pay for the **wedding** as we go without touching the four months saved.
Keep using the **phone AI** every day for fault codes and study.
feel: I'd feel **calm**, and a little **cheated**, because I've bet on AI and like it.
S0.quote: The chatbot told me the labeller fault was glue temperature, and we were running again in ten minutes instead of waiting an hour for the engineer.
fieldNote: Her calm rests on a **busy plant** and a clear path to technician.
She uses AI as a **practical tool**, valuing ten minutes saved over grand promises.
Refusing to **borrow for the wedding** shows her traditional, careful view of money.

steps.text: Keep running filler line three on early shifts at Brookfield
Use the phone chatbot to decode labeller fault codes
Finish the PLC course by March and apply for technician

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, this one I can actually picture. It's already starting at our place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best time in years to be someone who likes learning. I'd tell anyone at Brookfield who'd listen to get on the training list now. Online I'd probably share the course I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me and bad for some of my friends. The ordering and the shift planning go to software first, and Sandra's assistant probably isn't replaced when she leaves. On the floor we'd get a robot palletiser, maybe a robot on the case packer, and fewer operators per line. I want to be the one who sets those robots up, not the one they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Sandra this month and ask to shadow the engineers when the new palletiser goes in. I'd finish the PLC course and start a robotics module, paying the 600 myself if Brookfield won't. I'd also help at the church job club on Thursdays, for people losing shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A little guilty, because what feels like a ladder for me is a trapdoor for some of the people I work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you thinking of when you say trapdoor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, mostly, on the case packer. He's 45, steady as anything, and he's told me he can't get on with screens. If the robot comes for the packer, I'd want Brookfield to move him to the warehouse rather than let him go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lean toward free markets. Should anyone step in here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think the government should stop companies buying robots, that's how we stay competitive. But firms owe their people training first, and churches and families should look after people in between. Our vicar already runs that job club, and it does more good than a form at the benefits office.

say: I'd say it's the **best time** in years for people who like learning.
I'd urge everyone at Brookfield to join the **training list** now.
think: Ordering and **shift planning** move to software first, and office roles aren't replaced.
With a **robot palletiser** and fewer operators per line, I want to be the one setting robots up.
do: Ask to **shadow the engineers** when the new palletiser is installed this year.
Pay **600** for a robotics module if Brookfield won't fund it.
Help at the **church job club** on Thursdays for people losing shifts.
feel: I'd feel **excited**, with some **guilt** that my ladder is a trapdoor for others.
S1.quote: What feels like a ladder for me is a trapdoor for some of the people I work with.
fieldNote: She sees steady disruption as her **opportunity**, while naming who it hurts.
Her answer for Kofi is **redeployment**, not regulation, which fits her outlook.
She puts **church and family** where others might put the state.

steps.text: Shadow the engineers installing Brookfield's new robot palletiser
Pay 600 for a robotics module after the PLC course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the third picture. This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: learn the new stuff and get ahead of it. I'd probably post that robots arrive three years after the AI, so hands-on people have a window and should use it. At church I'd say we need to look after each other, because some families will be hit hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one rattles me. If AGI can do any thinking work by 2028, then programming the robots is thinking work too, so my technician plan stops being safe. By 2031 the robots can do my hands-on part as well. I'd be 32, newly married, and maybe with nothing a machine can't do cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two years before it lands, I'd still go hard at becoming a robot technician, because someone has to install and repair the hands-on robots until 2031 and maybe after. I'd shrink the wedding to fifty people in the church hall and put the difference, about 4,000, into savings. I'd ask Tom to think about which part of joinery a robot can't do, like fitting old houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, for the first time, honestly. I'm still making plans, but the plans feel shorter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the plans feel shorter. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Normally I plan in five-year steps: technician, then shift engineer, then a house and kids. In this picture I plan to 2031, and then I don't know. The church and the family would matter more, because those are the things a robot can't take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tom's work? It's hands-on like yours.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom fits kitchens into crooked old houses, which is about the hardest thing for a robot. I think he'd last longer than me. If it came to it, his wage would carry us, and I'd swallow my pride about that.

say: I'd post that robots arrive **three years** after AI, so hands-on workers should use that window.
At church I'd say we must **look after each other** through it.
think: Programming robots is **thinking work** too, so my technician plan stops being safe.
By **2031** I'd be 32, newly married, maybe with nothing a machine can't do.
do: Push hard to become a **robot technician** before the hands-on robots arrive in 2031.
Shrink the wedding to **fifty guests** and save the 4,000 difference.
Ask Tom to focus on **old-house fitting**, which robots struggle with.
feel: I'd feel **scared** for the first time, still planning, but with **shorter plans**.
S2.quote: If AGI can do any thinking work by 2028, then programming the robots is thinking work too, so my technician plan stops being safe.
fieldNote: Her early-adopter confidence breaks when she sees robot **programming** as thinking work.
She plans only to **2031**, a clear shrink from her usual five-year steps.
She'd lean on **Tom's wage** if needed, though it would hurt her pride.

steps.text: Train as a robot technician before the 2031 robot arrival
Cut the wedding to fifty guests in the church hall
Put the 4,000 saved on the wedding into savings
Rely on Tom's joinery wage if the line work goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, and robots by 2034. That's a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it straight: five years is a gift, don't waste it. I'd tell the younger operators to stop scrolling and start a course. I'd probably set up a little study group at Brookfield, Tuesdays after earlies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well out of this one. Robots by 2034 means seven years on the floor, and a few years in the middle as a technician, when every plant is installing robots and nobody knows how. That's the gold rush, and I'd want to be there with a toolbox.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the PLC certificate in 2027, the robotics one in 2028, and move into a technician job by 2029. We'd keep the wedding as planned next August, and buy a small house in 2029 on two wages. I'd keep five months of bills saved and never let the house deposit touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in a good way, if that's a thing. Like the night before a big changeover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You called it a gold rush. What happens after the robots are all in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I don't know. Once the robots are installed, a drinks plant probably needs one technician where it had ten operators. So I'd want to be one of the good ones, and maybe move into training people, which needs a human face for a while longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, yes, though I'd hate leaving my parents and the church. Tom says joiners can work anywhere. We'd look at the bigger industrial towns within an hour first, before anything further.

say: I'd tell people that **five years** is a gift, so don't waste it.
I'd start a **study group** at Brookfield on Tuesdays after earlies.
think: Robots by **2034** leave a few golden years for technicians installing them everywhere.
After installation a plant needs **one technician** where it had ten operators.
do: Gain the **PLC certificate** in 2027 and the robotics certificate in 2028.
Keep the **August wedding** and buy a small house in 2029 on two wages.
Hold **five months** of bills in savings, separate from the deposit.
feel: I'd feel **uneasy** in a good way, like the night before a big changeover.
S3.quote: Once the robots are installed, a drinks plant probably needs one technician where it had ten operators.
fieldNote: She frames the middle years as a **gold rush** for robot technicians.
She sees the **drop after installation** and plans to move into training others.
She'd **move** within an hour if needed, though family and church hold her.

steps.text: Get the PLC certificate in 2027 and robotics in 2028
Start a Tuesday study group for operators at Brookfield
Keep five months of bills saved apart from the deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth and last picture. This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. Robots at 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's plenty of time for anyone willing to work for it. I'd say it to my younger cousins especially: pick a trade now and keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is the comfortable one for me. I'd have a whole career as a technician before the robots come in 2039, and maybe move into engineering or training. My worry would shift to our kids, who'd be finishing school into a world with fewer ordinary jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd follow the same plan, certificates then technician, just without rushing. Tom and I would marry next August and try for a baby around 29. I'd open a small savings account for the children's training in the first year, even 50 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even. The fear moves from my job to my kids' jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future kids about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids to learn with their hands and their heads, and never think a job is forever. My grandad was a fisherman and my dad drove a lorry, and both of them had to change. Every generation changes, this one just changes faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a downside to having ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People like me get comfortable. I'd set a date every year to check whether my skills still pay. And the people who don't plan, like some of the operators on nights, would be hit just as hard in 2036 as in 2028.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** for anyone willing to work.
I'd tell my **younger cousins** to pick a trade now and keep learning.
think: I'd get a whole **technician career** before robots arrive in 2039.
My worry shifts to **our children**, who'd leave school into fewer ordinary jobs.
do: Follow the **certificate plan** to technician without rushing.
Marry Tom next August and **try for a baby** around 29.
Open a **children's training** savings account at 50 a month.
feel: I'd feel **calm** and **hopeful**, with the fear moving to my children.
S4.quote: I'd tell my kids to learn with their hands and their heads, and never think a job is forever.
fieldNote: With ten years, her fear moves from her own job to her **children's future**.
She guards against **coasting** with a yearly check on her skills.
She notes that people who **don't plan** get hit as hard either way.

steps.text: Work through the certificates to technician at a steady pace
Marry Tom next August and try for a baby around 29
Save 50 a month for the children's future training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes away the ladder I've been climbing before I reach the top. What would help is Brookfield paying for robot training for everyone on the floor, not just the keen ones, and honest dates from companies about when the machines are coming. I don't want handouts, I want a fair run at the next job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. People think it's old-fashioned, but my church is where folk would turn when the plants change, not an app. I'd want the people building these things to spend a Sunday in a church hall and see who they're changing.

headlineQuote: I don't want handouts, I want a fair run at the next job.
portrait: Nora is a **27-year-old filler-line operator** at Brookfield Drinks, engaged to Tom, a joiner.
She uses **AI tools daily** and studies PLCs at night, aiming for a technician job.
Traditional and careful with money, she **refuses to borrow** and leans on church and family.
She's calm in the slower pictures but **scared** when AGI by 2028 threatens her technician plan.
With ten years' warning, her worry moves to her **future children**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because it removes her technician **ladder** before she reaches the top.
whatWouldHelp: **Robot training** paid by Brookfield for everyone on the floor, not just the keen ones.
**Honest dates** from companies about when machines are coming.
